title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: From that day, natural philosophy — and chemistry in particular, in the broadest sense — became nearly my only occupation. I read eagerly the works of genius and insight that modern scientists had written. I attended lectures and cultivated the acquaintance of the university's men of science. I found even in Professor Krempe a great deal of sound knowledge and real information, despite his unpleasant appearance and manner. In Professor Waldman I found a true friend. His gentleness was never tainted by arrogance, and his teaching was delivered with such openness and good nature that it banished any hint of stuffiness. In a thousand ways he smoothed my path to knowledge, making the most complex subjects clear and accessible. My effort was unsteady at first, but it gained strength as I went on and soon became so intense that the stars often faded into morning light while I was still working in my laboratory.

Given my dedication, my progress was naturally rapid. My passion astonished the other students, and my skill impressed the professors. Professor Krempe often asked me, with a sly smile, how Cornelius Agrippa was getting along, while Professor Waldman expressed the greatest delight in my progress. Two years passed this way. I paid no visit to Geneva, being engaged heart and soul in pursuing discoveries I hoped to make. Only those who've experienced it can understand the pull of science. In other fields, you go as far as others have gone before, and there's nothing more to learn. But in science, there's always something new to discover and marvel at. A mind of moderate ability that closely pursues one subject must inevitably achieve great skill in it. And I, who continually chased a single goal with complete focus, improved so quickly that by the end of two years I'd made some discoveries in chemical instrumentation that earned me great recognition at the university. When I'd learned as much of the theory and practice of natural philosophy as any professor at Ingolstadt could teach me, staying there no longer helped my progress, so I thought of returning to my friends and my hometown — until an incident extended my stay.

One phenomenon had particularly captured my attention: the structure of the human body, and indeed any living creature. Where, I often asked myself, does the principle of life come from? It was a bold question, one that has always been considered a mystery. Yet how many truths hover just beyond our grasp, kept at bay only by our cowardice or carelessness? I thought this over and resolved to focus specifically on the branches of natural philosophy related to physiology. Without an almost supernatural passion, this study would have been unbearable. To examine the causes of life, we must first turn to death. I studied anatomy, but that wasn't enough. I also had to observe the natural decay and corruption of the human body. My father had been careful to ensure my mind was never haunted by supernatural fears. I'd never trembled at ghost stories or feared apparitions. Darkness had no effect on me. A graveyard was simply a place where bodies, once the seat of beauty and strength, became food for worms. Now I was led to examine the process of decay and forced to spend days and nights in vaults and charnel houses. I fixed my attention on every detail most repulsive to human feeling. I watched the fine form of man degrade and waste away. I saw the flush of life give way to the corruption of death. I watched how worms inherited the wonders of the eye and brain. I paused, examining and analyzing every detail of this transformation from life to death and death to life — until, from the midst of this darkness, a sudden light broke upon me. A light so brilliant and yet so simple that, while I was dizzy with the immensity of what it revealed, I was stunned that among so many brilliant scientists who had pursued the same questions, I alone should be the one to discover so astonishing a secret.

Remember, I'm not describing the ravings of a madman. The sun doesn't shine more certainly in the sky than this truth I'm about to tell you. Some miracle might have produced it, yet the stages of the discovery were clear and logical. After days and nights of incredible labor and exhaustion, I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life. More than that — I became capable of bringing lifeless matter to life.

The astonishment I first felt at this discovery soon gave way to delight and ecstasy. After so much painful work, to arrive at the summit of my desires was the most gratifying reward I could imagine. But the discovery was so immense and overwhelming that all the steps that had led me to it were wiped from my mind. I saw only the result. What the wisest men in history had sought since the creation of the world was now within my grasp. Not that it all opened before me at once, like a magic scene. The knowledge I'd gained was better suited to direct my efforts toward a goal than to present that goal as already achieved. I was like the Arabian in the Arabian Nights tale who was buried alive with the dead and found a passage back to life, aided only by one glimmering light that seemed useless.

I can see from your eagerness and the wonder and hope in your eyes, my friend, that you expect me to share this secret. I cannot. Listen patiently to the end of my story, and you'll easily understand why I hold back. I won't lead you, unguarded and passionate as I was then, to your destruction and certain misery. Learn from me — if not from my words, then from my example — how dangerous it is to acquire knowledge, and how much happier is the man who believes his hometown is the whole world than the one who tries to become greater than nature allows.

When I found such astonishing power in my hands, I hesitated a long time over how to use it. Although I could give life, preparing a body to receive it — with all its intricate fibers, muscles, and veins — remained enormously difficult. I debated whether to attempt a being like myself or something simpler. But my imagination was too inflamed by my first success to doubt my ability to create something as complex and wonderful as a human being. The materials I had seemed barely adequate for such an ambitious project, but I didn't doubt I would ultimately succeed. I prepared myself for countless setbacks. My work might be repeatedly thwarted, and the final result might be imperfect. Yet when I considered the daily improvements in science and technology, I was encouraged to hope that my present attempts would at least lay the foundation for future success. I couldn't let the magnitude and complexity of my plan serve as an argument against it. With these feelings, I began the creation of a human being. Since the smallness of the parts would greatly slow my work, I decided — contrary to my first intention — to make the being of enormous size: about eight feet tall and proportionally large. After making this decision and spending some months collecting and preparing my materials, I began.

No one can imagine the storm of feelings that drove me forward in those first days of success. Life and death seemed to me like imaginary boundaries I would break through first, flooding our dark world with light. A new species would bless me as its creator and source. Many happy and excellent beings would owe their existence to me. No father could deserve his children's gratitude as completely as I would deserve theirs. And if I could give life to dead matter, I might in time — though I now found it impossible — restore life where death had apparently given the body over to decay.

These thoughts sustained me while I pursued my work with relentless drive. My cheeks grew pale from study. My body wasted from confinement. Sometimes, on the very edge of success, I failed. Yet I still clung to the hope that the next day or the next hour might deliver the breakthrough. The hope I had dedicated myself to was a secret that I alone possessed. The moon watched over my midnight labors while, with breathless, unrelenting eagerness, I tracked nature to her hiding places. Who can imagine the horrors of my secret work as I dug among the foul dampness of graves or tortured living animals to give life to lifeless clay? My limbs tremble and my eyes blur at the memory. But then, a resistless, almost frantic impulse drove me on. I seemed to have lost all feeling except for this one pursuit. It was only a passing trance, and it made me feel all the more sharply once the unnatural stimulus wore off and my old self returned. I collected bones from charnel houses. With unholy fingers, I disturbed the deepest secrets of the human body. In a solitary room at the top of the house — really more of a cell, separated from all other rooms by a gallery and staircase — I kept my workshop of filthy creation. My eyes were nearly starting from their sockets as I labored over the details. The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse provided many of my materials. Often my humanity recoiled from my work. But still, driven by an eagerness that kept growing, I brought my creation near to completion.

The summer months passed while I was engaged, heart and soul, in this single pursuit. It was a beautiful season. The fields had never produced a more plentiful harvest, nor the vines a more abundant vintage. But my eyes were blind to nature's beauty. The same obsession that made me ignore the world around me also caused me to forget the friends who were so many miles away and whom I hadn't seen in so long. I knew my silence worried them. I remembered my father's words: "I know that while you're pleased with yourself, you'll think of us with affection, and we'll hear from you regularly. If your letters stop coming, I'll have to assume you're neglecting your other duties too."

I knew well how my father would feel, but I couldn't tear my thoughts from my work. It was loathsome in itself, yet it had seized an irresistible hold on my mind. I wanted, so to speak, to put off everything to do with my affections until the great project that consumed my every instinct was finished.

At the time I thought my father would be unfair to blame me for vice or weakness. But I'm now convinced he was right to suspect I wasn't entirely blameless. A perfect human being should always maintain a calm and peaceful mind and never let passion or fleeting desire disturb that peace. I don't think the pursuit of knowledge is an exception to this rule. If a study tends to weaken your affections and destroy your taste for those simple pleasures that nothing can taint, then that study is certainly wrong — unfit for the human mind. If this rule were always followed, if no one let any pursuit interfere with domestic love, Greece would not have been enslaved, Cæsar would have spared his country, America would have been discovered more gradually, and the empires of Mexico and Peru would not have been destroyed.
But I'm moralizing at the most exciting part of my tale, and your expression reminds me to continue.

My father didn't reproach me in his letters. He only noticed my silence by asking about my work in greater detail. Winter, spring, and summer passed during my labors. But I didn't watch the blossoms open or the leaves unfold — sights that had once given me supreme delight. I was that deeply absorbed. The leaves of that year had withered before my work neared completion. Every day showed me more clearly how well I had succeeded. But my enthusiasm was dampened by anxiety. I seemed more like a slave condemned to toil in the mines, or in some other unhealthy trade, than an artist at his beloved work. Every night I was gripped by a slow fever. I became nervously sensitive to a painful degree. The fall of a leaf startled me. I avoided other people as if I were guilty of a crime. Sometimes I was alarmed at the wreck I was becoming. Only the driving force of my purpose kept me going. My work would end soon, I told myself, and then exercise and recreation would cure my creeping illness. I promised myself both of these when my creation was complete.
